transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what’s been troubling you and what brings you in today?

Hi, yes, thank you for seeing me. Um, so... I came in because, well, my family kind of pushed me to make an appointment, but also because I know what’s been going on lately sounds really hard to explain to people who aren't in my exact situation. 

I work as an operations manager right now, and I’m also doing my MBA, which is a ton of networking and strategy, so you're always kind of reading between the lines anyway, trying to figure out where the market is going. But lately... well, I’ve been completely convinced that one of my MBA classmates and this startup advisor we work with are quietly coordinating these massive career opportunities for me behind the scenes. 

And I mean, I know how that sounds to say out loud, but it’s just so incredibly obvious when you actually look at the details. Like, they’ll make certain comments during a lecture, or they'll drop a message in our cohort Slack channel, and to anyone else, it probably just looks like a normal link to a business article or a generic comment about market scaling. But I can see that they are actually coded signals meant specifically for me. It's in the specific phrasing they use, or the emojis, telling me exactly where my career is supposed to go and what professional moves I need to make next. 

I've been spending hours—like, late into the night—just going back through the Slack threads, looking at the exact words they use and the timestamps, because it all lines up perfectly to guide my next career step. It’s like this secret, high-level mentorship they’ve set up just for me, but nobody else seems to get it when I try to show them the patterns in the messages. My roommate told me I was losing it and needed to talk to a doctor, but if you saw the threads, you'd see exactly how they are orchestrating everything...

So far, you’ve described these signals and messages as guiding you toward opportunities—do you feel these people are trying to help you, or have you noticed any signs that they might be trying to harm you or control you in any way?

Harm me? Oh, no, no, not at all. I mean, why would they? It’s definitely about helping me, or at least, like, positioning me for something really big. Because if you think about it, the startup advisor—he actually has this massive background in venture capital, specifically in the tech sector, which is exactly where I’ve been trying to pivot my career since I started the MBA program. So if he wanted to sabotage me or, I don't know, hold me back, he could literally just ignore me or give me a bad recommendation, right? 

But instead, he’s taking all this time to carefully weave these specific opportunities into the cohort’s Slack channel just for me to find. Like, just last Tuesday, he posted this whole thread about supply chain disruptions in emerging markets, and to anyone else, it’s just reading material for our macroeconomics module. But the way he phrased the third paragraph, talking about "agile operational leadership," it was a direct nod to a paper I wrote last semester. It’s definitely mentorship. I don't feel controlled at all, I just feel... selected, I guess? Like they see my raw potential. 

In operations management, which is what I do for my day job, you always have to identify bottlenecks and figure out how to optimize the whole system, and I really think they see me as someone who can optimize whatever massive project they are building behind the scenes. So, no, I haven't noticed anything malicious or controlling in the slightest. It’s just very, very exclusive. My roommate thinks the whole thing is manipulative because they aren't just saying it to my face, but she really just doesn't understand how high-level networking operates at this tier. If they wanted to control me, they’d just offer me a standard contract and make me sign some crazy strict non-compete agreement, you know? But this... this is about guiding me so I can make the right strategic choices on my own. They're just giving me the map.
Have you ever felt that you are being singled out in a way that makes you feel special or chosen for something bigger than yourself?

Well, yeah, absolutely. That’s actually exactly what it is. It’s like... well, like I said earlier, I know how it sounds to people who aren't in the loop, which is why I came in, because my family just doesn't get it. But yes, I feel completely chosen. 

I’ve been completely convinced that this MBA classmate of mine and the startup advisor are quietly coordinating these massive, life-changing opportunities just for me. It’s not just a feeling, it’s a whole system they’ve built around me. Like, I’ll be sitting in a lecture, and the classmate will make a comment about, say, market penetration strategies in Q3, and everyone else is just taking notes, but I know—I just know—that it’s a coded signal about a specific sector I need to be researching for my career. 

Or the Slack messages! I was telling you about the Slack messages. They drop these links or make these little comments, and on the surface, it’s just business jargon, right? But the phrasing, the timing... it’s all coded signals telling me exactly where my career is supposed to go next. It’s like I’ve been tapped for this elite, invisible fast-track program that nobody else even knows exists. 

And it makes sense, right? Because in operations, you’re always looking for the most efficient, high-yield asset to invest time into, and they’ve clearly identified me as that asset. So yes, "chosen for something bigger" is exactly the phrase I would use. It’s like I’m the centerpiece of this huge strategic operation they are running behind the scenes, and all I have to do is decode the map they’re giving me. It’s exhausting, honestly, staying up all night analyzing the timestamps and the word choices, but you don't just ignore it when people at that level single you out for something this huge. You just don't.
Have you ever experienced periods of time when your mood was extremely high, you felt very energetic, or you needed much less sleep than usual?

Oh, absolutely, yes. That’s... well, 'high' is an interesting word for it, but honestly, most days lately I’ve just felt unusually switched on. Like, completely dialed in. It’s this constant, buzzing optimism, you know? I wake up and I just feel this incredible drive because I know, I can just feel it in my bones, that I’m right on the edge of something huge. It’s like all the pieces of the board are finally moving into place for my career, and I have all this energy to just tackle everything—my day job, the MBA, analyzing all those messages I told you about. I’m just firing on all cylinders, and it feels amazing to be this sharp. 

But... I guess the flip side of that, and maybe this is why my roommate was getting so concerned, is that I have zero patience right now. Like, absolutely none. Because I'm moving so fast and seeing all these high-level connections, I end up snapping at people over the dumbest things. I’ll snap at my MBA teammates if they are lagging behind on a simple operations analysis, or I'll get completely short with my boyfriend over, like, a five-minute delay when we're trying to leave the apartment to get coffee. Just small delays that normally wouldn’t bother me at all, they suddenly feel like this massive, infuriating roadblock when I’m operating with this much momentum. 

It’s just... when you know you are on the precipice of a major career transition, and you have this elite network guiding you, you can't afford to be dragged down by people who are just dragging their feet. So yeah, it's this weird mix of feeling more optimistic and capable than I ever have in my entire life, but also just being so incredibly irritated that everyone else is moving at a snail's pace while I'm trying to execute on these massive plans.
Have you ever had a period of time when you felt down or hopeless nearly every day, lost interest in things you usually enjoy, or had trouble functioning normally for at least two weeks?

Down or hopeless? No. No, honestly, I don't think I've ever felt like that. I mean, sure, there are days when a project at work gets derailed—like last month when our main supplier for the packaging materials had a massive logistics failure and I had to spend three days rerouting everything through a secondary vendor at a fifteen percent markup. That was incredibly stressful, obviously, and I was frustrated, but it wasn't hopeless. In operations, you can't really afford to feel hopeless, you know? You just pivot. You find the bottleneck and you fix it. 

So, no, I’ve never had a period where I just couldn't function or lost interest in things. If anything, my problem is usually that I’m too interested in too many things at once. Like right now, between the day job, the MBA coursework, and keeping up with all the networking and the... the strategic mapping I was telling you about from the advisor, my plate is completely full. If I were the kind of person who just shut down or stayed in bed for two weeks, there is absolutely no way I could maintain my current trajectory. My calendar is literally color-coded down to the fifteen-minute increment just to keep everything moving forward. 

My boyfriend sometimes says I don't know how to relax, which, okay, maybe that's true, but that’s completely different from being depressed or down. I just like being productive. I like optimizing my time and pushing toward the next goal. So to answer your question, no, I've never had a two-week block where I just couldn't function or didn't want to do anything. I'd honestly go crazy if I had to sit still and do nothing for that long. I just have way too much momentum for something like that.

Have you ever experienced strange or unusual thoughts or perceptions that others around you don't seem to notice—like hearing voices, seeing things that aren't there, or believing something strongly that others don't understand?

Well, as far as believing things strongly that others don't understand, we already talked about the whole advisory network thing, and obviously my family and my roommate don't get that at all. But... you know, the hearing things part of your question is actually really interesting. I haven't really told anyone this because it sounds, well, I don't know how it sounds to someone on the outside, but yes. Yes, I have been experiencing something like that, though it's very specific. 

It’s not like a full conversation or anything. It usually happens a few times a week, almost always when I’m working really late. Because, like I mentioned, my schedule is completely packed right now, so I’m usually up until two or three in the morning at my desk, going over the operations plans for my day job or doing the heavy data modeling for my MBA classes. I have this whole setup with three monitors in the corner of our living room, and it'll be completely dead silent in the apartment—my roommate is always asleep by ten, she works in HR, completely different schedule—and out of nowhere, I will hear my name. Just clear as day. 

Or sometimes it’s a really short, sharp phrase, like... like "go now." Just like that. "Go now." And it is so incredibly clear, like the audio quality is just perfect, that I immediately snap out of my spreadsheets and look around the room. I’ll actually stop what I'm doing, pick up and check my phone, thinking maybe I left a podcast running on Spotify, or maybe an ad popped up on one of my browser tabs, or I'll even check to see if someone accidentally called me and I'm on speakerphone. But my phone is locked, the tabs are all just data dashboards, and there is absolutely no one there. 

It's just... it's so vivid. I literally search the room every single time because it sounds like someone is standing right behind my ergonomic chair. I usually just end up sitting back down and thinking, okay, well, maybe it's just my brain telling me to keep pushing, keep executing on the strategy, you know? Because I am so dialed in right now and moving so fast. But yeah, to answer your question, a few times a week I hear that, and it's so real I check my phone every single time.

Have you ever believed that you have special powers, abilities, or a unique role that sets you apart from others, beyond what you've already described about being selected for this career opportunity?

Special powers? Like, supernatural stuff? No. No, definitely not. I mean, I'm an operations manager, so my entire brain is wired for logic, empirical data, and measurable outcomes. If I can't track it in a KPI dashboard or map it out in a Gantt chart, it doesn't really exist for me, you know? So I don't think I have any magical abilities, like reading minds or predicting the future or anything crazy like that. 

I just have a really, really high capacity for complex problem-solving right now. Some people might look at my schedule—like my roommate, who is constantly asking how I'm surviving on so little sleep while balancing the MBA, my full-time job, and all the strategic networking for this upcoming transition—and they might say, "Oh, she’s superhuman." But it's not a superpower. It's literally just extreme discipline and optimization. I built this completely customized Notion workspace that integrates my calendar, my project milestones, and my communication logs, and I use a modified Pomodoro technique to just blast through the busywork. 

So when I look at a supply chain bottleneck and instantly see the redundancies, which my MBA teammates always struggle with for some reason, it’s not because I have a special power. It’s just trained analytical thinking that is firing at absolute peak efficiency right now. I can just see the moving parts faster than other people can. 

So yeah, aside from the fact that this advisory network has specifically identified me because they recognize my strategic value and my potential for this transition, there's nothing supernatural going on. It’s all grounded in my actual, real-world capabilities and my drive to execute. I don't need special powers when I have this level of momentum and a perfectly optimized workflow.

Have you ever believed that you have a unique role or importance that goes beyond what others would consider reasonable—like you’re destined for a world-changing mission or have a special connection to events that others aren’t aware of?

A world-changing mission? No, definitely not. I mean, I'm not out here trying to, you know, solve climate change or invent a new form of renewable energy or anything like that. I think people throw around words like "destiny" and "world-changing" way too much these days, especially in the corporate and startup spaces. 

You go to these networking events—which, by the way, I have to attend at least two a week right now for my MBA program, usually downtown, which is an absolute nightmare for parking, so I have this whole system where I book a spot three days in advance on an app to save time—but anyway, you go to these events and you hear these guys talking about how their new B2B SaaS platform is going to "change the world." And I always just think, it's not changing the world, Brad, it's just streamlining payroll. 

I'm very realistic about my lane. My role, even with this advisory network specifically selecting me for this upcoming transition, is about high-level corporate strategy and operational efficiency. It's important, yes, and it's a massive step up for my career trajectory, but I'm not... I'm not the chosen one in some sci-fi movie, you know? I don't have any secret connection to global events. Like, when the news is on, it's just the news. I analyze it for market trends, obviously. Like last week when there was that issue with the shipping lanes overseas, I immediately started looking at how it would impact our Q3 freight costs, because that's just how my brain works. I mapped out three different contingency plans before my boss even brought it up in the Monday stand-up. 

But I don't think the shipping lane was blocked *for* me, or that I have some, like, spiritual connection to global trade events. It's just data. It's all just inputs and outputs that I need to manage. So, no, I don't have any grand ideas about saving humanity or being on a world-changing mission. I just want to run the most efficient operations division in the sector, leverage this advisory opportunity to its absolute maximum potential, and finish my MBA with top marks. That's my mission. It's highly specific, it's measurable, and it's definitely grounded in reality.
Have you ever felt that your importance or abilities are far greater than others realize, to the point where you believe you are operating at a level that most people could never understand?

Um, no, I wouldn't phrase it like that at all. I don't think my abilities are... incomprehensible, or that I'm vastly more important than anyone else. Like I was saying before about the whole superpower thing, it really just comes down to systems and momentum. 

For example, in my operations role, we use this enterprise resource planning software, and most people just use the default dashboards. Which is fine, but it's incredibly inefficient. So I spent maybe four hours last weekend completely remapping the API integrations so it feeds directly into my custom tracking sheets. My boss, Greg, looked at it on Wednesday and he was totally blown away, asking how I even managed to build it because it was so far ahead of what the IT guys gave us. 

But it's not that he couldn't understand it. If I sat down with Greg for twenty minutes and walked him through the logic pathways and the automation scripts I wrote, he would absolutely get it. He just doesn't have the time to do it himself, and frankly, he doesn't have the hyper-focus that I have right now.

So, it's not that I'm operating on some mystical, unreachable plane of existence. I'm just putting in the hours. I'm operating at a high capacity, sure, but anyone could do it if they optimized their life the way I have. I mean, my roommate thinks it is ridiculous that I meal-prep exactly fourteen portions of chicken and quinoa every Sunday at 4 PM so I don't waste time cooking during the week, but that's just basic time management. It's not that she is incapable of understanding it, she just chooses to relax and watch TV instead. 

So, no, I don't feel like I'm fundamentally more important or doing things that are beyond human comprehension. I just have really, really good metrics right now and a solid work ethic.
Have you ever had a period lasting several days where your mood was unusually high, you felt extremely confident or irritable, and you were doing or saying things that were out of character for you?

Well, I wouldn't say "out of character," exactly, because I've always been a highly driven person, but... I will say that lately, yeah, most days I’ve just felt unusually switched on. Like, completely dialed in. It’s this massive wave of optimism that hits me the second I wake up—usually around 3:30 or 4:00 AM, completely refreshed—and I just have this intense feeling like I’m right on the edge of something huge. It’s hard to describe, but it’s like the feeling you get right before a massive product launch when all the QA testing is done and you just *know* the metrics are going to blow past the quarterly projections. Everything just feels aligned and electric. 

But, you did mention irritability, and... okay, I guess I have to admit that my tolerance for other people's friction has pretty much evaporated. Because I'm operating with this incredible momentum, when people slow me down, I have been snapping at them. Like, my MBA teammates or my boyfriend, Mark. And over really small delays that normally wouldn’t bother me at all. 

Like, for example, on Thursday, my teammate Sarah was supposed to upload her section of our corporate finance risk analysis by 8:00 PM. It got to 8:12 PM, and she hadn't synced the document, so I just went off on her in the WhatsApp group. I sent this whole paragraph about how a twelve-minute delay on a deliverables handover in the real world cascades into massive financial losses and that her lack of urgency was a liability to our operational flow. Which, I mean, is true, but normally I would have just sent a polite ping. 

And then with Mark, just yesterday morning, he couldn't find his car keys. It delayed us leaving the apartment by maybe three or four minutes. Usually, I'd just help him look, maybe joke about it, but I actually yelled at him. I gave him this whole lecture about his lack of spatial organization and how he desperately needs to establish a dedicated staging area for his everyday carry items so we don't bleed time on basic logistics. He just stared at me. So, yeah, I am feeling incredibly optimistic and sharp, but when you're moving at this speed, those tiny little speed bumps just feel infuriating.
Have you noticed your performance at work or in your MBA program suffering because of your focus on these messages or your increased irritability?

Suffering? I mean... I guess it depends on what metrics you're looking at. Because in my mind, my actual output is higher than ever, but... okay, yes, there has been some fallout. I'll admit that. 

For instance, Greg, my manager—who I mentioned earlier, the one who was supposedly so impressed by my API work—he actually pulled me into a formal one-on-one meeting on Tuesday. And he had this whole document prepared. He has actually started officially documenting what he called missed handoffs and unreliable follow-through. Which is just... it's so short-sighted. Yes, technically, I didn't send the standard end-of-day summary emails on Monday or Wednesday, but that's only because I was completely absorbed in restructuring our entire Q4 logistics pipeline! But he doesn't see the macro vision, he just sees that a few standard micro-tasks weren't checked off his little list. So now there's this official paper trail questioning my reliability, which is incredibly frustrating.

And then in my MBA program, it’s bleeding over there, too. Remember I told you about Sarah and the WhatsApp incident? Well, she apparently complained to our corporate finance professor. Not just about my communication style, but because I ended up completely rewriting her section of the group assignment before I submitted it. Her projections were just way too conservative given the momentum I'm seeing in the market, so I fixed it to reflect reality. But the professor actually pulled me aside after the lecture and explicitly questioned my judgment on the assignment. He said my risk models were erratic and that I was alienating my cohort. 

So... yeah. I am still showing up to everything. I'm at the office early every single day, I haven't missed a lecture, I'm still doing all the work. But my relationships at the office and at school are getting so strained right now. Everyone is just pushing back so hard, and the friction is getting to a point where... well, it's why I felt I needed to get some help, or at least talk to someone. Because even though I feel like I'm operating perfectly, the people around me are clearly having issues with it, and I absolutely cannot afford to let this derail my career trajectory or my degree.
Have you ever felt that your ability to function in your daily life—like at work, school, or with relationships—has been significantly impaired because of these experiences?

Well, like I was just touching on, I guess that’s exactly what’s happening, even if I really hate the word 'impaired.' Because in my head, I’m functioning better than ever, but... functionally, in the real world? Yeah, things are hitting a wall. 

It’s exactly like I mentioned with Greg. The fact that my manager has actually started a formal paper trail, officially documenting what he calls my missed handoffs and unreliable follow-through... I mean, that is a massive red flag for my career. In operations management, if you have a documented history of being unreliable, it doesn't matter if you're a visionary who completely overhauled the API integrations. You become a liability to the corporate structure. 

And it’s the exact same dynamic in my MBA program right now. When my professor pulled me aside to question my judgment on that group assignment after I rewrote Sarah's section, it wasn't just a casual academic critique. He was genuinely concerned about how I was operating and interacting with the rest of the cohort. 

So, I mean... I’m still showing up. I haven't missed a single day of work, I haven't skipped a class, I am physically present and doing a massive amount of labor. But the pushback is just constant now. My relationships at work and at school are getting so incredibly strained, just... fraying at the edges, because everyone thinks I'm the one who is out of step. It’s like I’m a gear spinning at ten thousand RPM and everyone else is barely moving, and the whole machine is just smoking because we aren't meshing. 

And it got to the point where I just... I had to admit that this level of friction is completely unsustainable. That’s really why I felt I needed to get some help, or at least come in and talk to you today. Because I absolutely cannot let this ruin my degree or derail my promotion timeline, even if I still fundamentally believe they're all just moving too slow.
Have you ever had a period of time when you felt so down or hopeless that you stopped caring about work, school, or things you usually enjoy, even for just a few days?

Down or hopeless? Um... no. No, honestly, that’s not really something I deal with at all. I mean, I know what you’re talking about, like when people just sort of... check out? I’ve seen it with some of the people on my logistics teams, where they just lose all their motivation and let their metrics completely tank because they’re in some kind of personal slump. But for me? No, I’ve never had a period where I just stop caring about work or school. If anything, my baseline is the exact opposite. 

Even when things are incredibly stressful—like right now, with Greg breathing down my neck and documenting my so-called missed handoffs, or my professor questioning my group assignment—I don’t get hopeless. I don't shut down. I get... well, I get fired up. I want to fix it, I want to optimize the situation and prove my models are correct. The idea of just staying in bed or not caring about my career trajectory is completely foreign to me. I’ve always been the kind of person who has a five-year plan, a ten-year plan, and a structural contingency for both. 

Like, I remember back in my undergrad, when I was balancing a full credit load and a really demanding supply chain internship... there were days that were physically exhausting, sure, just because of the sheer volume of hours I was putting in. But I never lost interest. I never stopped caring about the end goal. I think if I ever stopped caring about my output, I wouldn't even know who I was anymore, because my drive is so deeply tied to how I operate in the world. 

So, yeah, feeling down or hopeless for days at a time and just giving up on my deliverables or the things I enjoy? That just doesn't happen to me. I don't really have a 'give up' gear. I just keep moving forward. I always have to be moving forward, no matter what kind of friction I'm dealing with.
Have you ever questioned whether the messages or signals you’ve been interpreting might not actually be intended for you or might not be real?

Questioning it... yeah. Actually, yes, and that’s a huge part of why I’m sitting here right now. Because I came in today specifically because I know this sounds hard to explain. I really do. I’m an operations manager, I deal in hard data and logistics, so I know exactly how this sounds to an outside observer. But for weeks now, I’ve been completely, absolutely convinced that one of my MBA classmates—not Sarah, someone else in my cohort who has a lot of venture capital connections—and this startup advisor I met at a tech mixer last month are quietly coordinating opportunities for me. 

Like, the way it happens feels so undeniably real. I’ll be sitting in our advanced corporate strategy lecture, and my classmate will make a very specific, deliberate comment about, say, "aggressive market entry." And then, maybe two hours later, that startup advisor will drop a message in our local tech incubator Slack channel using that exact same phrasing. "Aggressive entry." And I’ve been reading these as coded signals about where my career is supposed to go. It’s like they are testing my strategic readiness for some massive executive role they’re building out behind the scenes, leaving these breadcrumbs for me to follow. 

But then... I do have these moments. These moments where the analytical side of my brain kicks in and I step back and think, wait, is this actually happening? Are two people who barely know each other really coordinating this elaborate recruitment test just for me, or am I just connecting dots that aren't actually there? Because logically, I know it sounds like a massive stretch. I know it sounds like something out of a spy movie rather than standard corporate recruiting. 

But when you're in the middle of it, and the data points just keep lining up perfectly—like the timestamps on those Slack messages matching the exact themes of our class discussions—it is so incredibly hard to just dismiss it as a coincidence. It feels so deliberate, so intentional. So I’m caught between being completely convinced that this incredible hidden track is being laid out for my career, and this terrifying thought that maybe I'm completely misinterpreting standard networking chatter. And I just... I needed to run it by someone, because it's exhausting trying to figure out if the signals are real or if my brain is just working overtime and making up the entire puzzle.

Have you ever had a period lasting several days where you felt unusually energetic, needed much less sleep, and found yourself making impulsive decisions or behaving in ways that were out of character for you?

Well, energetic is... yeah, definitely. I mean, for the last few weeks, most days I’ve just felt unusually switched on. That's the best way I can describe it. It’s like my brain is fully optimized, running without any lag whatsoever. I’ll wake up after maybe three or four hours of sleep, and I don't even need to hit snooze, I don't even need coffee, I am just instantly up and mapping out my entire day on the whiteboard in my home office. I’ve just been feeling so incredibly optimistic, you know? It’s this constant, buzzing feeling like I’m right on the edge of something huge, like all my career plans and these signals I’m picking up on are about to culminate into this massive breakthrough. 

But... the flip side of that, and I guess this ties into the "out of character" part of your question, is that I have absolutely zero patience right now. None. Because I am moving so fast and feeling so capable, I find myself just snapping at people. I'll snap at my logistics teammates, or even my boyfriend, over these tiny, small delays that normally wouldn’t bother me at all. 

Like, just the other day, my boyfriend—he's usually great, very supportive—but he was taking maybe two extra minutes to find his keys before we were supposed to leave for dinner. Normally, whatever, I'd just check my emails while I wait. But I just completely lost it. I snapped at him, pacing by the door, lecturing him about how horribly inefficient his daily systems are and how he needs to implement a dedicated spatial organization protocol for his personal items. I was genuinely furious over two minutes. 

And it’s happening at work, too. If a teammate takes more than ten minutes to reply to a message about a routine vendor update, I am immediately jumping down their throat, just tearing into them about how they're creating operational bottlenecks. I usually pride myself on my professional communication—you have to in management—but lately, these microscopic delays just make my skin crawl. It’s like, I’m so optimistic and ready for this huge next step, but everyone else is just dragging their feet, and I can't stop myself from lashing out at them for it. So, yeah, the snapping is probably out of character, even if the energy itself just feels like I'm finally operating at my true capacity.
Have you felt that your insights, abilities, or role in these messages are so superior that you are above the need for standard processes, rules, or feedback from others?

Superior? Above the rules? Oh, no, no, no. Definitely not. If anything, it’s the exact opposite. I mean, you have to understand, my entire professional foundation is built on standard processes. I live and breathe SOPs—Standard Operating Procedures. The idea of just throwing out the rulebook or ignoring feedback goes against everything I stand for as an operations manager. I mean, how can you even measure success without a baseline, right? You need KPIs, you need structured feedback loops. 

Even when I’m getting frustrated with my team, like I was saying earlier about the bottlenecks and snapping at people, it’s actually *because* I want them to follow the processes more efficiently. It's not because I think the processes shouldn't apply to me. I'm just annoyed that they aren't executing the protocols at the speed I know we're capable of. 

And with these messages, the signals I was telling you about with the startup advisor and my classmate? I don’t see it as me being superior or above the system at all. I just see it as... a different system. Like a specialized, high-level recruitment track. But a track still has rails, you know? It’s still a process. They are testing me, which inherently means I am subject to their evaluation and their rules. If I thought I was above it all, I wouldn't be spending hours analyzing the timestamps on the Slack channel to make sure I’m interpreting their feedback correctly. 

I actually value feedback immensely. I thrive on 360-degree reviews, peer evaluations, agile retrospectives, all of it. I mean, sure, I feel incredibly capable right now, like my brain is firing on all cylinders and I'm ready for this massive executive jump, but that doesn't mean I get to just skip the steps. You can't optimize a system by breaking it. You optimize it by understanding the constraints and working perfectly within them. So, no, I definitely don't feel like I'm above the need for rules or feedback from others. If anything, I’m probably hyper-focused on making sure I’m following the *right* rules for this specific hidden opportunity they're laying out for me. I just... I need the framework. Without a framework, it's just chaos, and I absolutely do not do chaos.

Questioning it... yeah. Actually, yes, and that’s a huge part of why I’m sitting here right now. Because I came in today specifically because I know this sounds hard to explain. I really do. I’m an operations manager, I deal in hard data and logistics, so I know exactly how this sounds to an outside observer. But for weeks now, I’ve been completely, absolutely convinced that one of my MBA classmates—not Sarah, someone else in my cohort who has a lot of venture capital connections—and this startup advisor I met at a tech mixer last month are quietly coordinating opportunities for me. 

Like, the way it happens feels so undeniably real. I’ll be sitting in our advanced corporate strategy lecture, and my classmate will make a very specific, deliberate comment about, say, "aggressive market entry." And then, maybe two hours later, that startup advisor will drop a message in our local tech incubator Slack channel using that exact same phrasing. "Aggressive entry." And I’ve been reading these as coded signals about where my career is supposed to go. It’s like they are testing my strategic readiness for some massive executive role they’re building out behind the scenes, leaving these breadcrumbs for me to follow. 

But then... I do have these moments. These moments where the analytical side of my brain kicks in and I step back and think, wait, is this actually happening? Are two people who barely know each other really coordinating this elaborate recruitment test just for me, or am I just connecting dots that aren't actually there? Because logically, I know it sounds like a massive stretch. I know it sounds like something out of a spy movie rather than standard corporate recruiting. 

But when you're in the middle of it, and the data points just keep lining up perfectly—like the timestamps on those Slack messages matching the exact themes of our class discussions—it is so incredibly hard to just dismiss it as a coincidence. It feels so deliberate, so intentional. So I’m caught between being completely convinced that this incredible hidden track is being laid out for my career, and this terrifying thought that maybe I'm completely misinterpreting standard networking chatter. And I just... I needed to run it by someone, because it's exhausting trying to figure out if the signals are real or if my brain is just working overtime and making up the entire puzzle.

Destined for greatness? Like... a special mission? No, no, definitely not. That sounds like something out of a fantasy novel or a superhero movie, right? I really don't believe in destiny at all, actually. I mean, destiny implies that things just happen to you, or that there's some predetermined path that requires zero input, zero structural planning, and zero optimization. And that just goes against everything I stand for. As an operations manager, we don't rely on destiny. We rely on actionable metrics, strategic foresight, and relentless execution. 

I mean, do I think I'm going to be highly successful? Yes, absolutely. But that's not because I'm "destined" for it or because I have some mystical mission nobody else can do. It's because I have a meticulously crafted five-year career trajectory. I have a spreadsheet that tracks my professional milestones, my networking touchpoints, my MBA coursework progress, and my quarterly performance reviews. I earn my success through pure efficiency and hard work. If I'm going to be great—which, you know, I fully intend to reach the C-suite by the time I'm thirty-two—it's going to be because I built the infrastructure to get myself there, not because the universe just handed it to me.

And as for a mission no one else can fulfill... no. I mean, the whole point of a good system is that it's replicable. If I'm doing my job right, I should be able to train someone else to do it. Now, are there people who can do it as *well* as I can right now, with my current energy levels and my capacity to process information? Maybe not many. Like I said, I'm operating at peak capacity, catching all those subtle recruitment signals I told you about earlier. But I don't think it's some exclusive, magical mission. It's just high-level corporate headhunting. If someone tried to tell me my career goals weren't real, I wouldn't need to defend a "destiny." I'd just pull up my laptop and show them my data. I'd point to my KPIs. 

So, no, I don't have any magical destiny or chosen-one complex or whatever you'd call it. I just have a very, very solid plan, and I happen to be executing it flawlessly right now.
